findings.title: Content pages declare no canonical URL
findings.evidence: 21 of 21 sampled content pages carry no rel=canonical link. Without one, a crawler that reaches the same content through a different URL, for example with a tracking parameter or a trailing slash, has to guess which address is the real one. Examples: https://books.toscrape.com/, https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/1000-places-to-see-before-you-die_1/index.html, https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/category/books/add-a-comment_18/index.html.

evidence_detail.method: presence of a parsed rel=canonical link on sampled content pages
evidence_detail.expected: a self-referencing canonical on every content page

suggested_action.summary: Add a self-referencing rel=canonical to every content template, pointing at the absolute preferred URL of that page.
how: Emit the canonical from the route's own definition so it is always the page's preferred absolute URL.
Use the same scheme, host and trailing-slash form as the sitemap, so the two do not disagree.
suggested_action.mechanism: A canonical consolidates the signals for one piece of content onto one address. Without it, parameterised and duplicated variants compete with each other and none accumulates the full weight.
suggested_action.verification: Request each URL and confirm the canonical matches the URL that was requested.

findings.title: No robots.txt is published
findings.evidence: A request for https://books.toscrape.com/robots.txt returned 404. No robots.txt means no crawler restrictions, so this does not block anything. It does mean there is nowhere to declare a sitemap or to state a deliberate policy for training versus retrieval crawlers.

evidence_detail.method: single request for /robots.txt recorded in the snapshot

suggested_action.summary: Publish a robots.txt that declares the sitemap and states an explicit policy for training and retrieval crawlers.
how: Add a Sitemap: line pointing at the sitemap index.
Decide deliberately whether to allow training crawlers; leaving it undeclared is a decision made by default rather than on purpose.
Keep retrieval and user-triggered agents allowed unless there is a specific reason not to.
suggested_action.mechanism: Absence does not shut the discovered gate, but it forfeits the one place to declare a sitemap and to record an intentional crawler policy, so a future change can silently remove citation eligibility.
suggested_action.verification: Request /robots.txt and confirm a 200 with text/plain and a resolvable Sitemap line.

findings.title: No usable sitemap was found
findings.evidence: No sitemap could be read. Locations tried: https://books.toscrape.com/sitemap.xml (status 404), https://books.toscrape.com/sitemap_index.xml (status 404), https://books.toscrape.com/sitemap-index.xml (status 404). Discovery fell back to following links, which found 412 URLs. This is a crawl-efficiency problem rather than a block: pages linked from the site are still reachable.

evidence_detail.method: sitemap locations from robots.txt, then conventional paths
evidence_detail.expected: at least one sitemap returning 200 and parsing as a urlset

suggested_action.summary: Publish a sitemap with accurate lastmod values and declare it in robots.txt.
how: Generate a sitemap from the publishing pipeline so lastmod reflects the real content change date rather than the build clock.
Segment it by template (products, articles, static pages) so a crawler can recrawl the fast-changing parts without refetching the rest.
Add a `Sitemap:` line to robots.txt pointing at the index.
suggested_action.mechanism: A sitemap does not unblock anything; it tells a crawler which URLs exist and which have changed, so pages that are weakly linked internally get discovered and changed pages get recrawled sooner.
suggested_action.verification: Fetch the sitemap URL and confirm it returns 200, parses, and lists the canonical URL of every template.
